strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a simple training objective combining conventional SFT with confidence-guided interpolation of output logits and targets. The method requires no additional annotations or proprietary-model scoring of training examples.

The same-backbone, same-dataset comparisons consistently favor SFTMix across both model families and both instruction-following datasets. Table 1 reports MT-Bench overall gains of approximately 0.20–0.29 points and AlpacaEval-2 length-controlled win-rate gains of 0.32–1.67 percentage points.
The medical experiments provide complementary evidence beyond LLM-based judging: macro-average accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral, respectively.

The ablations provide useful evidence for retaining the NTP objective and using Mixup as a modest regularizer. Comparable results using a smaller reference model are encouraging. Public datasets and backbones, several training hyperparameters, and evaluation standard errors are documented.
weaknesses: The central contribution of confidence-guided pairing is insufficiently isolated. There is no random-pairing or within-confidence pairing control on the same dataset, nor a comparison against confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.4 changes the training responses and lacks a confidence-guided comparator on that modified corpus, so its results cannot establish that training dynamics are crucial. This unresolved attribution issue is the main reason for a Borderline Findings assessment.

The proposed mechanism remains speculative. Figure 2's t-SNE visualization and illustrative examples do not establish that confident examples are overfitted, or that SFTMix specifically improves generalization in unconfident regions. Equation 4 interpolates output logits; the claimed smoothing of semantic decision boundaries and transfer of supervision require direct evidence, such as held-out performance and train–validation gaps stratified by confidence.

The uncertainty estimates cover repeated evaluation, with no reported independent training runs. They therefore do not establish robustness to training randomness. Some improvements are also small relative to the reported evaluation errors: Mistral on Alpaca improves from 9.18 ± 0.17 to 9.50 ± 0.28 in length-controlled win rate. Claims of significant improvement need appropriately paired uncertainty estimates and a clearly specified tuning protocol.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including checkpoint selection, pair construction and reshuffling, loss reduction and normalization, sequence-length handling, and exact generation and judge configurations. No implementation link is provided. Equation 2 defines mean negative log-likelihood rather than perplexity; averaging these different quantities across checkpoints can produce different confidence rankings, so the implemented definition needs clarification.

The computational motivation is not supported by end-to-end cost measurements. Reference-model training and checkpoint scoring introduce additional work that should be included in comparisons. The smaller-reference experiment is useful, but experiments on three datasets of different compositions do not establish scalability to datasets of any size.

The broader contribution needs sharper positioning. Park and Caragea (2022), which already combines data cartography with Mixup, receives little substantive discussion. Comparisons with ordinary Mixup and relevant inexpensive regularizers such as NEFTune would clarify the benefit of this particular adaptation and strengthen the main-conference case.
